Neonatal Western hognose snakes (Heterodon nasicus) emerge from parchment-shelled eggs after an incubation period that depends critically on substrate temperature. For eggs maintained at a constant 24.5 °C [T = 24.5 °C], the mean age at hatching is 56 days [ab = 56 days], though field records indicate a natural range of 49 to 63 days depending on local thermal regimes. Newly emerged hatchlings, which rely exclusively on their internal yolk reserves during the first days post-eclosion, exhibit a wet mass at birth of 2.3 grams [Wwb = 2.3 grams]. This modest initial body mass is typical for colubrid snakes of this lineage and reflects the limited space within the yolk-laden egg for provisioning larger neonates. Female hatchlings, in particular, emerge at a mean total length of 18 centimeters [Lb = 18 centimeters] from snout to vent, with a broader population range extending from 13 to 23 centimeters depending on maternal investment and incubation conditions. This neonatal size establishes the foundation for the pronounced sexual size dimorphism that characterizes adult Heterodon nasicus populations.

Sexual maturation in Heterodon nasicus proceeds according to a well-defined schedule under controlled thermal conditions. When maintained at a stable temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the time since birth at puberty is 730 days [tp = 730 days], a duration that corresponds to roughly two years of post-hatching growth and development. This relatively protracted juvenile phase allows individuals to accumulate sufficient body reserves before transitioning to a reproductively active adult state. The attainment of gonadal activation marks a critical life-history transition, after which both sexes become capable of participating in the annual breeding cycle. The species exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism in ultimate body size, a pattern common among colubrid snakes where females attain considerably larger dimensions than males. The ultimate total length for female Heterodon nasicus reaches 154 centimeters [Li = 154 centimeters] from snout to vent, while the ultimate total length for male conspecifics is substantially more modest at 66.3 centimeters [Li = 66.3 centimeters]. This nearly 2.5-fold difference in asymptotic length between the sexes has significant implications for reproductive output, as larger body size in females permits the production of larger clutches and contributes to the species' overall fecundity.

The maximum recorded adult body mass in Heterodon nasicus provides additional insight into the species' life-history strategy. Based on the known scaling relationship between length and mass, the ultimate wet weight for females is estimated at 1498 grams [Wwi = 1498 grams], a value consistent with the large body size achieved by mature individuals. This substantial somatic investment underpins the species' reproductive potential, as gravid females must allocate considerable resources to egg production. Under optimal thermal conditions maintained at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the maximum reproductive rate is realized through a combination of clutch size and clutch frequency. Females typically lay 13 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 13 eggs per clutch] and produce a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], a modest reproductive output relative to many other colubrids. This low annual fecundity is balanced by the relatively large size of individual hatchlings, which enhances neonatal survival during the critical early weeks of independent life. The incubation temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C] represents an optimized thermal regime that balances developmental speed with hatching success.

Longevity records for Heterodon nasicus indicate a remarkably extended lifespan for a snake of this body size, particularly given the species' relatively slow pace of life. Under captive conditions maintained at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan reaches 19.8 years [am = 19.8 years], a duration that places this species among the longer-lived members of the North American colubrid fauna. This extended biological lifespan, equivalent to approximately 7227 days, reflects a conservative life-history strategy characterized by delayed maturity, modest annual reproductive output, and sustained somatic maintenance across multiple decades. The combination of a prolonged juvenile phase, late age at first reproduction, and relatively low fecundity per reproductive event aligns with predictions from life-history theory for species occupying stable, resource-predictable environments where adult survival is favored over high annual fecundity. Field-based estimates from mark-recapture studies suggest somewhat shorter longevity in wild populations, likely due to predation pressure and environmental stochasticity, but the species' physiological capacity for extended survival is clearly demonstrated.

Comparative analysis of reproductive timing and body size scaling in Heterodon nasicus reveals interesting contrasts with other North American colubrids of similar adult dimensions. The relationship between neonatal length and ultimate female length, with hatchlings measuring approximately 18 centimeters [Lb = approximately 18 centimeters] and adult females reaching 154 centimeters [Li = 154 centimeters], yields a growth multiplier of roughly 8.5-fold, a value that aligns closely with allometric expectations for snakes with this general body plan. The relationship between neonatal and adult mass in H. nasicus, with an ~650-fold increase from 2.3 grams to 1498 grams, is consistent with isometric scaling and implies that shape changes during ontogeny are minimal. The two-year interval between hatching and puberty, corresponding to 730 days [tp = 730 days] since birth at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], is typical for colubrids of this size and reflects the need to reach a minimum body size threshold before reproductive allocation becomes energetically feasible. This delayed maturation, combined with the species' maximum lifespan of 19.8 years [am = 19.8 years], produces a generation time that is long relative to body size, a pattern that has important implications for population dynamics and conservation planning at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C].
